title: Beer Hangover: Why It Feels Different and How to Avoid It
excerpt: Why beer hangovers feel heavy and bloated rather than sharp, why IPAs hit harder, the best beers for avoiding a hangover, whether non-alcoholic beer can cause one, and how to recover.
metaDescription: Why beer hangovers feel different, why IPAs hit harder, the best beer for no hangover, whether NA beer can cause one, and how to recover faster.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** a beer hangover feels different from a liquor hangover mostly because of *how* you drink beer, not because beer contains some special hangover chemical. Beer is dilute, so a night on it means a lot of liquid, a lot of carbonation, a full stomach, and often more total alcohol than you'd guess, especially if the beer is a 7% IPA in a 16-ounce glass. Beer is actually lower in congeners (the by-products that make bourbon and brandy hangovers worse) than many dark spirits and red wine. So the typical beer hangover is a heavy, foggy, bloated one rather than a pounding, nauseous one. The amount of alcohol is still what decides how bad it gets.

**The quick rules:** Count alcohol, not glasses. Check the ABV (alcohol by volume) on the can or menu, because a strong craft pint can be nearly two standard drinks. Eat before and while you drink, alternate with water or a non-alcoholic beer, and slow down after the first two or three. If you want a beer night with the least fallout, choose session-strength or light beers, or swap in non-alcoholic beer for part of the evening.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research on alcohol and hangovers. It is not a substitute for a doctor who knows your health history. **Get help right away** if someone who has been drinking is confused, can't stay awake, is vomiting repeatedly, has slow or irregular breathing, or has cold, clammy, or bluish skin. Those are signs of alcohol poisoning, not a hangover. In the US, call 911. If you take prescription medication, are pregnant, or have liver, kidney, or heart problems, talk to your doctor about whether and how much you can safely drink.

## What a Hangover Actually Is

Before getting into beer specifically, it helps to know what's going on in a hangover in general, because most of it applies to every drink.

A hangover is the set of symptoms that shows up as your blood alcohol falls back toward zero: headache, tiredness, thirst, nausea, a sour stomach, poor concentration, sensitivity to light and sound, and low mood. Researchers still don't have a single explanation, but the main contributors are well understood:

- **Poor sleep.** Alcohol helps you fall asleep but breaks up sleep in the second half of the night and cuts into REM sleep. A lot of the next-day fog is simple sleep debt. (We go deeper on this in our guide to [alcohol and REM sleep](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-rem-sleep-complete-scientific-analysis-2025).)
- **Inflammation.** Heavy drinking triggers an immune response, and studies have linked hangover severity to markers of inflammation. This may explain part of the "flu-like" feeling.
- **Acetaldehyde.** Your liver turns alcohol into acetaldehyde, a toxic compound, and then breaks that down into harmless acetate. If you drink faster than your body can keep up, acetaldehyde exposure goes up.
- **Fluid loss.** Alcohol suppresses a hormone (vasopressin, also called antidiuretic hormone) that tells your kidneys to hold on to water, so you urinate more. Dehydration contributes to thirst, dry mouth, and headache, although research suggests it isn't the whole story.
- **Stomach irritation.** Alcohol irritates the stomach lining and increases acid, which feeds nausea and that queasy morning feeling.
- **Congeners.** These are other compounds produced during fermentation and aging, such as methanol, fusel alcohols, and various aldehydes. Drinks with more of them tend to produce worse hangovers at the same amount of alcohol.

If you want the full science, our [hangover science hub](/never-hungover/complete-hangover-science-hub-2025) covers each of these in detail. For beer, the interesting part is how the drink itself changes the mix.

## Why Beer Hangovers Feel Different

### 1. Volume: you drink a lot more liquid

A standard drink in the US contains about 14 grams of pure alcohol. That's roughly 12 ounces of 5% beer, 5 ounces of 12% wine, or 1.5 ounces of 40% liquor. To get the same alcohol from beer, you drink eight times the liquid you would from a shot.

That volume does a few things at once:

- **You feel full and bloated.** Several pints of carbonated liquid stretch the stomach, which is part of why a beer hangover often comes with a heavy, gassy, sluggish gut.
- **You urinate a lot.** Some of that is just the volume going through. Some is the alcohol's effect on your kidneys. Either way, you spend the night going back and forth to the bathroom, and you may wake up thirsty despite having drunk "so much."
- **It's easy to lose count.** People track beers by the round, not by the ounce. Four pints in a long evening doesn't feel like much, but four 16-ounce pints of 5% beer is more than five standard drinks.

### 2. Carbonation: alcohol may reach your blood faster

Carbonated drinks seem to speed up how fast alcohol gets into the bloodstream, probably by moving the drink out of the stomach and into the small intestine sooner, which is where most absorption happens. Most of the research here looks at sparkling wine and mixers rather than beer, and the studies are small, so the size of the effect is uncertain and varies a lot from person to person. Beer's lower carbonation compared with champagne, and the fact that it's usually sipped over time, may blunt this. Still, it's one reason people say beer "sneaks up" on them in a way they don't expect. Our [champagne hangover guide](/never-hungover/champagne-hangover-why-it-happens-prevention-guide) covers the bubbles question more fully.

### 3. Fewer congeners than dark liquor

This is the part that works in beer's favor. Congeners are a real factor in hangover severity. The best-known study, by Rohsenow and colleagues in *Alcoholism: Clinical and Experimental Research* (2010), gave people either bourbon (high in congeners) or vodka (very low in congeners) at the same high dose. Bourbon produced worse hangovers, although the alcohol dose itself still produced most of the misery.

Older research ranking drinks by congener content placed brandy, red wine, rum, and whiskey at the top, with white wine, gin, and vodka near the bottom. Beer generally sits in the low-to-moderate range, closer to white wine than to bourbon. Very dark, strong, or barrel-aged beers likely carry more congeners than a pale lager, but nobody has done careful hangover studies comparing beer styles to each other, so treat that as a reasonable guess rather than a proven fact.

The practical point: beer isn't a "dirty" drink in the way dark spirits are. When a beer hangover is bad, it's almost always the quantity.

### 4. The pace is slower, but the night is longer

Beer is usually drunk slowly, which gives your liver more time to keep up. Your body clears roughly one standard drink per hour, though that varies widely between people. Slow sipping is good. The trouble is that beer nights also tend to be *long*: a game, a brewery tour, a festival, a wedding. Six hours of steady beer can easily add up to eight or ten drinks without anyone ever feeling like they were drinking fast.

### 5. It often comes with salty food and late nights

Beer pairs with wings, pizza, and pretzels, and beer nights often run late. Salty food makes you thirstier. Late nights cut into sleep. Neither is beer's fault, but both show up in the morning.

## The IPA and Craft Beer Problem

If you've noticed that craft beer nights hit harder than nights on light lager, you're not imagining it. The main reason is simple: **craft beers tend to be much stronger.**

| Beer style | Typical ABV | Standard drinks in 12 oz | Standard drinks in a 16 oz pint |
|---|---|---|---|
| Non-alcoholic beer | 0.5% or less | under 0.1 | about 0.1 |
| Light lager | about 4% | about 0.8 | about 1.1 |
| Regular lager or pilsner | about 5% | 1.0 | about 1.3 |
| Standard IPA | 6 to 7% | 1.2 to 1.4 | 1.6 to 1.9 |
| Double / imperial IPA | 8 to 10% | 1.6 to 2.0 | 2.1 to 2.7 |
| Imperial stout, barleywine | 9 to 12% | 1.8 to 2.4 | 2.4 to 3.2 |

*ABV ranges are typical for each style and vary by brewery. Standard drinks are calculated against the US standard of 14 g of alcohol (12 oz at 5%).*

Look at that table again with a typical brewery night in mind. Four pints of 7% IPA is about seven and a half standard drinks. Four pints of 4% light lager is about four and a half. Same number of glasses, very different morning.

Craft beer also often comes in bigger servings. Many breweries pour 16-ounce or even 20-ounce glasses, and 16-ounce "tallboy" cans of hazy IPA are standard. A single tallboy of an 8% double IPA is more than two standard drinks.

### Is it the hops?

People sometimes blame hops for IPA hangovers. There is no good evidence that hops cause hangovers. Hops are a plant that adds bitterness and aroma, and the amounts in beer are small. The more likely explanations are the higher alcohol content, the bigger pours, and the fact that strong, flavorful beers are easy to drink slowly but steadily for hours.

### Is it the yeast, gluten, or "unfiltered" beer?

Hazy and unfiltered beers contain more yeast and protein, and some people say they feel worse after them. This hasn't been studied in any meaningful way. Gluten doesn't cause hangovers in people who tolerate gluten, though people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity can have real symptoms from beer that overlap with a hangover. If one particular beer style reliably makes you feel worse even at modest amounts, it may be worth paying attention to, but the alcohol math explains most of the IPA effect.

For a broader look at how craft and mass-market beers differ in ingredients and processing, see our analysis of [craft beer vs mass-market beer](/never-hungover/craft-beer-vs-mass-market-health-differences-study-2025).

## Does Beer Dehydrate You Less Than Liquor?

Per drink, probably yes, but not as much as people hope.

Because beer comes with so much water, its overall effect on your fluid balance is milder than the same alcohol taken as straight liquor. Studies on rehydration after exercise, many from Ronald Maughan's group at Loughborough University in the UK, found that beer with very little alcohol (around 2% or less) rehydrated people about as well as other drinks, while beer at around 4% led to noticeably more urine output. In other words, the alcohol in regular beer still pushes fluid out, and stronger beer pushes harder.

What this means in practice:

- Low-alcohol and non-alcoholic beer are genuinely hydrating.
- Regular-strength beer is not dehydrating per glass in the dramatic way spirits are, but it isn't a hydrating drink either.
- Strong craft beers behave more like wine in this respect.
- Drinking water between beers still makes a difference, mostly because it slows you down.

Dehydration also isn't the whole hangover. You can wake up fully hydrated and still feel terrible because of poor sleep, inflammation, and the alcohol dose itself. Water helps; it doesn't cure.

## Best Beer for No Hangover: What Actually Works

There is no hangover-proof beer. But some choices give you much better odds than others. Here they are, roughly in order of how much they help.

### 1. Lower-alcohol beer is the biggest lever

Since the amount of alcohol drives hangover severity more than anything else, the most effective "best beer to avoid a hangover" is simply a weaker one. Session IPAs, light lagers, and table beers in the 3 to 4.5% range let you drink at the same social pace while taking in a third to half less alcohol than a 7% IPA.

### 2. Pale over very dark and strong (a small edge)

Lighter, cleaner styles like pilsners, lagers, and pale ales probably carry fewer congeners than imperial stouts, barrel-aged beers, and barleywines. That's a small edge at best, and those dark styles are also much stronger, which matters more. If you're choosing between a 5% pilsner and a 12% barrel-aged stout, the stout is the worse bet for both reasons.

### 3. Smaller pours

Order the 10- or 12-ounce pour instead of the 16- or 20-ounce. Choose flights over full pints at a brewery. Smaller glasses are one of the easiest ways to cut total alcohol without feeling like you're cutting back.

### 4. Non-alcoholic beer for part of the night

This might be the most underrated tool. Switching to non-alcoholic beer after your second or third drink keeps a beer in your hand and keeps you in the rhythm of the night, while your liver catches up. NA beers have improved a lot in recent years, and many breweries now make NA versions of IPAs, lagers, and stouts.

### 5. Food, water, and pacing

None of these is specific to beer, but they all matter. Eat a real meal before you start, because food in your stomach slows how fast alcohol gets into your blood. Alternate with water or NA beer. Aim to stay around one standard drink per hour or slower. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) goes through each step.

We also rank common drinks from least to most hangover-prone in our guide to the [least hangover alcohol](/never-hungover/least-hangover-alcohol-ranked).

## Non-Alcoholic Beer: Can It Give You a Hangover?

For practical purposes, no.

In the US, beer labeled "non-alcoholic" can contain up to 0.5% alcohol by volume, and many brands contain less. Beers labeled "alcohol-free" in some countries are held to a lower limit, often 0.05%. At 0.5%, a 12-ounce NA beer contains about one-tenth of a standard drink. You'd need to drink around ten of them to equal one regular beer, and your liver clears that small amount as fast as you drink it. Your blood alcohol never rises meaningfully.

That doesn't mean you'll always feel great the morning after a night of NA beer. If you do feel rough, the more likely reasons are:

- **Poor sleep** from a late night, noise, or a full bladder.
- **Lots of liquid and carbonation**, which can leave you bloated.
- **Salty or heavy food** eaten alongside it.
- **Individual sensitivity** to ingredients such as gluten for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

One important caveat: people who are pregnant, in recovery from alcohol use disorder, or taking medications that interact badly with any alcohol (such as disulfiram) should talk to their doctor before drinking NA beer, since "non-alcoholic" does not always mean zero.

## Does Mixing Beer and Liquor Make It Worse?

The old rhyme "beer before liquor, never been sicker" has been tested. A randomized trial by Köchling and colleagues in the *American Journal of Clinical Nutrition* (2019) had volunteers drink beer then wine, wine then beer, or only one of the two. The order made no meaningful difference to hangover severity. What predicted a worse hangover was how drunk people got and whether they vomited.

Mixing drinks probably gets its bad reputation because nights that involve beer *and* shots *and* wine are usually nights with more total alcohol. Our [beer before liquor myth](/never-hungover/beer-before-liquor-myth) guide covers the research in more detail.

## What a Beer Hangover Typically Feels Like

Everyone's hangovers are a little different, but people commonly describe beer hangovers this way:

- **Bloated and gassy**, with a heavy stomach.
- **Foggy and sluggish** rather than sharply sick.
- **A dull headache**, often worse with dehydration and poor sleep.
- **Thirsty**, despite having drunk a lot of liquid.
- **Frequent bathroom trips** overnight, which wreck sleep.

Hangovers after strong craft beer can feel more like a classic wine or liquor hangover, with more nausea and a sharper headache, which fits with the higher alcohol dose. If headaches are your main problem, our guide to [alcohol headaches](/never-hungover/alcohol-headache-why-it-happens-how-to-prevent-2025) explains the main triggers.

## How to Recover From a Beer Hangover

Time is the only real cure. Your body needs to clear the alcohol and its by-products, catch up on sleep, and let your stomach settle. These steps help you feel better while that happens.

1. **Rehydrate steadily.** Sip water through the morning. If you were sweating, vomiting, or had a very long night, an oral rehydration drink or electrolyte mix helps replace sodium and potassium. Our roundup of the [best hangover recovery drinks](/never-hungover/best-hangover-recovery-drinks) compares options.
2. **Eat something gentle.** Toast, crackers, bananas, eggs, or a simple broth-based soup can steady your blood sugar and settle your stomach. Greasy food the morning after doesn't "soak up" alcohol, since by then it's already in your bloodstream, but if it sounds good and sits well, there's no harm.
3. **Get more sleep if you can.** A nap often does more than any remedy.
4. **Be careful with painkillers.** Acetaminophen (Tylenol) carries liver risks when combined with heavy or regular drinking, and anti-inflammatories like ibuprofen and naproxen can irritate a stomach that alcohol already upset. If you use one, take a single label dose with food and water. Read our guides on [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) and [Aleve (naproxen) and alcohol](/never-hungover/aleve-and-alcohol) before you reach for either, and ask a pharmacist if you take other medicines.
5. **Skip "hair of the dog."** Another beer may take the edge off briefly by delaying the drop in blood alcohol, but it only pushes the hangover later and adds to the total.
6. **Move gently.** A walk and fresh air can help you feel more human. Hard exercise while you're dehydrated and short on sleep is not a great idea.

If a hangover lasts much longer than a day, see our guide on [two-day hangovers](/never-hungover/two-day-hangover) for why that happens and when it's worth talking to a doctor.

## Where DHM Fits (and Where It Doesn't)

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a compound from the Japanese raisin tree (*Hovenia dulcis*), a plant used in traditional East Asian hangover remedies. A widely cited study by Shen and colleagues in the *Journal of Neuroscience* (2012) found that DHM reduced signs of alcohol intoxication and withdrawal in rats, apparently by acting on GABA receptors in the brain. Later animal research has looked at DHM's effects on how the liver processes alcohol and acetaldehyde.

The honest summary: everything above comes from rodents, and no good human trial has tested DHM on hangovers. Some people find DHM helpful as one part of a routine, typically taken with water during or after drinking. It is not a substitute for pacing, food, water, and sleep, and it does not lower your blood alcohol or make it safe to drive.

If you want to try it on a beer night, a straightforward single-ingredient product such as [Double Wood Supplements DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20) is a reasonable place to start. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers timing and amounts. If you take prescription medications, check with your doctor or pharmacist first.

## A Simple Plan for a Big Beer Night

Here's what this all adds up to for a brewery visit, a game, a festival, or a wedding:

- **Before:** eat a real meal with some protein and fat. Drink a glass of water. Decide roughly how many drinks you're aiming for.
- **Choosing beer:** start with something you really want, then move to a session beer, a light lager, or an NA beer. Check the ABV on every menu.
- **Serving size:** order smaller pours or flights when you can. Count a 16-ounce IPA as about two drinks.
- **Pacing:** aim for about one standard drink an hour or slower. Have a glass of water or an NA beer between rounds.
- **Late night:** stop drinking alcohol a couple of hours before bed so your sleep has a chance to recover. Drink water before you sleep.
- **Morning:** water or electrolytes, a gentle breakfast, more sleep if possible, and cautious use of painkillers.

## Beer Culture Without the Hangover

Beer is a social drink in most of the world, and a lot of beer culture is built around long, slow sessions. In Germany, the classic beer hall serving is a full liter, and in Britain the pint is the default. Our guides to [German beer culture](/never-hungover/german-beer-culture-guide) and [British pub culture](/never-hungover/british-pub-culture-guide) cover how to enjoy both traditions while keeping your next day intact. The common thread is simple: the hangover follows the total alcohol, and beer makes it easy to drink more of it than you meant to.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Why do beer hangovers feel different from liquor hangovers?**

Mostly because of how much you drink and how fast. Beer is dilute, so a night of beer usually means a lot of liquid, a lot of bathroom trips, a bloated stomach, and sometimes more total alcohol than you realize. Beer is also lower in congeners (the by-products that make dark liquors worse) than bourbon, brandy, or red wine, so the hangover tends to feel heavy and dull rather than sharp. The single biggest factor is still the total amount of alcohol.

**Are IPA hangovers worse than lager hangovers?**

Often, yes, but mainly because IPAs are stronger. A typical lager is around 4 to 5% alcohol, while many IPAs run 6 to 7% and double IPAs reach 8% or more. A 16-ounce pint of 7% IPA holds close to two standard drinks. Hops themselves have no good evidence of causing hangovers. Count drinks by alcohol, not by glasses.

**What is the best beer to drink to avoid a hangover?**

No beer is hangover-free, but lower-alcohol beers give you the best odds. Light lagers, session beers (roughly 4% or less), and non-alcoholic beers let you drink at a social pace while taking in much less alcohol. Paler beers are generally lower in congeners than very dark, strong styles, though the difference is small next to the effect of the alcohol itself.

**Can non-alcoholic beer give you a hangover?**

Practically, no. In the US, non-alcoholic beer can contain up to 0.5% alcohol, and many brands contain less. You would need to drink around ten of them to match the alcohol in one regular beer, and your body clears that small amount as you go. If you feel off after NA beer, the likely causes are poor sleep, dehydration, a big meal, or sensitivity to something else in the drink, not alcohol.

**Does beer dehydrate you less than liquor?**

Per drink, beer is somewhat less dehydrating because you take in a lot of water along with the alcohol, and research on rehydration suggests low-strength beer (around 2% or less) behaves close to water. Stronger beers still make you urinate more than the liquid alone would explain, and a long night of beer means many bathroom trips. Drinking water between beers still helps.

**Does mixing beer and liquor make a hangover worse?**

Not by itself. A 2019 randomized trial in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition found that drinking beer before wine, or wine before beer, did not change hangover severity. Mixing tends to go badly because it usually means drinking more and faster. The total amount of alcohol matters far more than the order.

**Can DHM help with a beer hangover?**

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound that has shown effects on alcohol intoxication and alcohol metabolism in animal studies, and a small amount of human research. Human evidence on hangovers is still limited, so treat it as a possible helper, not a guarantee. It does not lower your blood alcohol, does not make it safe to drive, and does not replace pacing, food, water, and sleep.

**How long does a beer hangover last?**

Most hangovers ease within 24 hours, with the worst of it in the morning when blood alcohol has returned to zero. Very heavy drinking, poor sleep, and getting older can make symptoms drag on longer. If you are vomiting repeatedly, can't keep fluids down, are confused, or feel much worse than a normal hangover, get medical help.
